title: Cataconacke (Old Field)
summary: Cataconacke, recorded by Tooker as Cataconnock, refers to Great Neck near Setauket, now known as Old Field. The existing map point marks the modern Old Field peninsula as a general location for the placename.
address_label: 207 Old Field Rd, Setauket- East Setauket, NY 11733
activity_update_summary: Corrected the Cataconacke history with exact pages, the 1667 boundary-marking testimony, and a link to Sasarataicko's biography.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Cataconacke preserves a Setauket-area name for the Old Field peninsula, interpreted as a limited or enclosed place, land, or field. The meaning fits a neck of land bounded by water and shows how Native placenames could describe the shape and use of a landscape. North Shore peninsulas carry Native geographies and older names beneath later English estates and village landmarks.
history_content: John A. Strong describes the 1659 Cataconacke/Old Field negotiations as involving John Mahue, Wyandanch, and Wyandanch's advisors Checonow/Cockenoe and Sasarataicko/Sassakataka. A 1667 deposition records that Wyandanch appointed Sakkatakka and Chekanno to mark the tract. The deposition calls Pauquatoun—not Sasarataicko—the former chief counselor. [1. John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011), p. 51; Gaynell Stone, ed., The History and Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), p. 199.] Read Sasarataicko's biography.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Cataconacke, Cataconnock, and the related Cometico. The name is interpreted as describing a limited or enclosed place, land, or field, fitting a neck of land bounded by water.

Why Place Names Matter

“The names of places, the names that people give to the land, the rivers, the towns, and the cities, contain miniature history lessons, stories wrapped up in a few words.”

— Minnesota Historical Society Press, Minnesota Place Names: A Geographical Encyclopedia (2001), Publisher description
land_loss_content: In 1666, Brookhaven records describe a deed for Great Neck, naming the neck as Cataconocke and connecting the transaction with Wyandance. The full deed text should remain in the reference record rather than the public body copy.
whereintheworld_content: Cataconacke shows how an Indigenous placename, a colonial deed name, and the modern Old Field landscape refer to the same neck of land. Keeping Cometico linked here helps avoid splitting one place into duplicate map records.
